records.table: Jack Daniel's Old No. 7 is the Tennessee whiskey from Lynchburg, dripped through ten feet of sugar maple charcoal before it goes into new charred oak. It pours at 80 proof with caramel, vanilla and a light spice, neat, over ice or long with cola.
records.story: The house dates its distillery to 1866 and prints that year on its label; a biographer's reading of the land and deed records points to 1875, and the question stays open. Jasper Newton Daniel, known as Jack (died 1911), learnt to make whiskey as a boy on the farm of Dan Call, a preacher and distiller near Lynchburg, from Nathan Green, called Nearest, an enslaved man born about 1820 who later worked for Jack as his head distiller. The distillery has since named Green its first master distiller. Jack had no children, and in 1907 he handed the business to his nephew Lem Motlow (1869 to 1947). Prohibition, first the state's and then the nation's, stopped distilling in Lynchburg; Motlow worked for repeal, and the stills ran again from 1938. Brown-Forman bought the distillery in 1956. Old No. 7 was bottled at 90 proof after Prohibition, at 86 from 1987 and later at 80. Where the name came from nobody knows: the house tells several stories, and an old tax district number is the account most often given. For a bartender it is the bottle that teaches the style: the charcoal before the barrel is what keeps it from being sold as bourbon.

records.table: George Dickel Signature Recipe, the bottling long sold as George Dickel No. 12, is the Tennessee whisky from Cascade Hollow, chilled before it meets the maple charcoal. At 90 proof it gives vanilla, sweet corn and brown sugar, and its label spells whisky without the e.
records.story: George A. Dickel (died 1894) and his firm sold the whisky of the Cascade distillery in Cascade Hollow, near Tullahoma, founded by others in 1877 though its bottles claimed 1870, and the firm in time took a share in it and became its sole distributor. Tennessee's prohibition closed the hollow. In 1937 Schenley bought the Cascade trademark and the recipe, and in 1958, once the voters of Coffee County allowed it, the company sent a distiller to build a new distillery in the hollow. Its first mash ran in July 1959, and George Dickel Tennessee Whisky was first bottled in 1964. The house spells whisky without the e and has done so from the start: by its own account George Dickel meant it to stand beside Scotch. It chills the new spirit before the charcoal, from the old belief that whisky made in winter tasted mellower, and lets the cold spirit fill the charcoal vats rather than drip through them. The numbered bottlings were later renamed, No. 12 becoming Signature Recipe. For a bartender the bottle is the contrast to Jack Daniel's: the same state and the same law, a different way with the charcoal.

records.story: The label honours Nathan Green, called Nearest, born about 1820, an enslaved man hired out to Dan Call, a preacher, grocer and distiller near Lynchburg. Green taught the young Jack Daniel to make whiskey and later worked for him as head distiller, and the Jack Daniel distillery has since named him its first master distiller. Uncle Nearest 1856 went on sale in July 2017, by the brand's own launch notice, and the 1856 of its name is the year the brand dates itself back to, from its own research rather than settled record. Its early bottlings were sourced whiskey, made at other Tennessee distilleries and passed through the Lincoln County Process before ageing. In 2017 Bedford County approved the use of the old Sand Creek Farms at Shelbyville for the brand's home, and the Nearest Green Distillery opened there in 2019. Two accounts say that from 2022 the 1856 was whiskey the brand distilled, aged and bottled itself. For a bartender the bottle carries the story a guest at a Tennessee whiskey shelf should hear: whiskey making in Lynchburg was taught by an enslaved man, and his name is on this label.

It runs through sugar maple charcoal, is bottled at 91 proof for the year its founder died, and pours with caramel, vanilla and nutmeg.
records.story: Charles Nelson (died 1891) came to Nashville shortly before the Civil War, by the house's account, and from about 1870 ran the Green Brier distillery at Greenbrier, in Robertson County, north of the city. After his death in 1891 his widow ran the business until Tennessee adopted statewide prohibition in 1909 and the distillery closed its doors. The brand did not come back when national Prohibition ended. More than a century later two brothers, descendants of Charles Nelson, revived the name in Nashville. Their distillery in Marathon Village filled its first barrel of Tennessee whiskey on 16 August 2014 and opened to visitors that November. In 2017 the house released First 108, a two-year-old whiskey of its own make, sold only at the distillery. The flagship Tennessee whiskey followed from full-size barrels, sold at first in the Nashville market and bottled at 91 proof, a nod to the year Charles Nelson died. It is wheated, as the family recipe was, and it passes through sugar maple charcoal before ageing. For a bartender it is the wheated Tennessee whiskey and a lesson in how prohibition broke the state's distilling for a generation.

records.story: The founder set up Prichard's Distillery in 1997, by the house's own account, and its home is a former schoolhouse at Kelso, in Lincoln County; the house dates the opening of the distillery there to 1999, while other accounts give 1997. The label carries the name of a forebear who, by the family's account, made whiskey in Davidson County from white corn and spring water in pot stills, and whose will of 1822 left his still and its tubs to a son. The house made its Tennessee whiskey in copper pot stills and without the maple charcoal step that Jack Daniel's and George Dickel use. In May 2014 it opened a second distillery in Nashville, on the grounds of the Fontanel Mansion. When Tennessee wrote its definition of Tennessee whiskey into law in 2013, requiring the maple charcoal before ageing, the law carried an exception drawn by county and date, and the state's attorney general read it in 2015 as covering one distillery: Prichard's. For a bartender the bottle is the exception that teaches the rule: pour it beside Jack Daniel's Old No. 7 and a guest tastes what the charcoal does.
